questions: Are the movements involuntary?
Do you remain fully conscious and aware during the movements?
Are the movements repetitive and rhythmic?
Do the movements mainly involve the abdomen or diaphragm?
Do you have difficulty breathing during the episodes?
Did these movements begin after starting or increasing metoclopramide, domperidone, prochlorperazine, or another anti-nausea medication?
Did they begin after starting an antipsychotic medication?
Can you temporarily suppress the movements when asked?
Do the movements stop completely when you are asleep?
Do you have abdominal pain?
Are you confused or disoriented when you are not moving?
Have you had a recent fever or infection?
Did these movements begin suddenly, over minutes to hours?
Did they begin after a head injury or stroke?
Do you have weakness or loss of sensation on one side of your body?
Do the movements include grimacing, tongue movements, lip smacking, or chewing motions?
Have you had urinary incontinence or bitten your tongue during an episode?
Have you recently used cocaine, amphetamines, levodopa, lithium, or other recreational or neurologic drugs?
Do you have diabetes or unusually high blood glucose?
Have you had similar episodes previously?
orders: Bedside capillary blood glucose and serum beta-hydroxybutyrate
Serum electrolytes, measured serum osmolality, renal function, and HbA1c
Noncontrast CT head focused on the basal ganglia
MRI brain with diffusion-weighted and T1/T2/FLAIR sequences focused on the basal ganglia

Therapeutic trial of controlled correction of hyperglycaemia with subcutaneous insulin, targeting blood glucose 1.0–1.4 g/L, with serial neurological examinations over 24–48 hours to assess whether the involuntary movements resolve.
